title: Best PC and Gaming Monitors UK
short: Gaming, ultrawide, curved and portable monitors compared by refresh rate, panel type and resolution.
intro: The right monitor depends on what you'll use it for: gaming wants a high refresh rate and low response time, creative work wants colour accuracy, and general use benefits most from strong contrast. This guide compares monitors tested by Tom's Hardware, using their own instrumented contrast and colour measurements rather than just impressions.

products.name: 49-Inch Odyssey G9
products.best_for: Buyers who want maximum immersion and desk real estate
products.summary: An enormous ultrawide effectively combining two 27in 1440p screens, with a tight 1000R curve and accurate colour out of the box. Tom's Hardware measured 2,152.9:1 contrast after calibration, though it has no motion blur reduction and no built-in speakers.
pros: Accurate colour out of the box

products.name: S3222DGM
products.best_for: Gamers who want strong contrast and value in one screen
products.summary: Tom's Hardware's pick for gaming, with a sharp, vivid and accurate image and premium-level contrast measured at 4,000:1, a third better than its rated spec. Also praised for general productivity use, though it lacks HDR.
pros: Sharp image with vivid, accurate colour

products.name: AW3423DWF
products.best_for: Buyers who want the best possible image quality in an ultrawide
products.summary: A QD-OLED ultrawide with stunning SDR and HDR images, deep contrast, a wide colour gamut and calibration dialled in straight out of the box. Tom's Hardware found no flaws of consequence, at a premium price.

products.name: Odyssey Neo G8
products.best_for: Buyers who want 4K resolution with fast refresh and deep contrast
products.summary: Combines Mini LED lighting with a Quantum Dot film for contrast Tom's Hardware measured at 25,000:1, far above a typical VA panel, at a rare 4K/240Hz combination, though colour gamut volume is only average.
pros: Colour accurate out of the box

products.name: P2712V
products.best_for: Buyers who want 4K and high refresh gaming without a high price
products.summary: A dual-mode monitor offering 4K at 160Hz or 1080p at 320Hz, with accurate colour out of the box and premium video processing. Tom's Hardware calls it terrific value, though brightness and colour gamut are only average and it lacks USB ports or speakers.
pros: Premium video processing, low motion blur
cons: No USB ports or internal speakers

products.name: AW3225QF
products.best_for: Buyers who want the best possible 4K gaming experience
products.summary: A 32in QD-OLED panel with a 240Hz refresh rate and Dolby Vision support, giving unmatched contrast, rich colour and perfect motion resolution with low input lag. Tom's Hardware found no flaws of consequence.
pros: Stunning image with broad contrast and rich colour
Greater colour volume than most other OLEDs
Perfect motion resolution, low input lag

products.name: UR59C
products.best_for: Productivity-focused buyers who want 4K without a gaming price tag
products.summary: A budget-friendly curved 4K monitor with quality build and effective curvature, though it needs calibration out of the box (colour error dropped from 4.3dE to 0.9dE once calibrated) and has no USB ports or adaptive sync.
cons: Needs calibration out of the box

products.name: NG17FGQ
products.best_for: Buyers who want a high-refresh second screen for travel
products.summary: A portable monitor with a rare combination of large-for-portable size and a 300Hz refresh rate over USB-C (240Hz via HDMI), solid build quality and accurate colour once calibrated, though it needs a capable GPU to actually hit 300Hz.
pros: Impressive video processing and game performance
cons: No extended colour or dynamic contrast for HDR
Can be tricky to run at full 300Hz

guide.q: What refresh rate do I need?
guide.a: For general use and office work, 60Hz is fine. For gaming, aim for at least 100Hz for a noticeably smoother feel, with 144-240Hz suiting competitive or fast-paced games. Very high refresh rates (300Hz+) mainly benefit competitive esports players with a GPU capable of hitting those frame rates.

guide.q: TN, IPS, VA or OLED panel?
guide.a: As a rough hierarchy for image quality: TN is the weakest but cheapest and fastest, IPS gives good colour and viewing angles, VA gives stronger contrast than IPS, and OLED gives the best contrast and colour of all, with near-instant response times, at a premium price.

1080p is the practical minimum today. 1440p is a popular middle ground between sharpness and easier-to-drive frame rates for gaming. 4K gives the sharpest image but needs a powerful GPU to run demanding games at high frame rates.

guide.q: Do I need FreeSync or G-Sync?
guide.a: Adaptive sync technologies like FreeSync (AMD) and G-Sync (Nvidia) match the monitor's refresh rate to your GPU's frame rate, reducing screen tearing and stutter. Check compatibility with your specific graphics card, since some monitors only officially support one standard, even if they often work with both in practice.
